title: The Role of Data (the “Oil of the 21st Century”)
subtitle: The most valuable resource of the digital age
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Data is often called the new oil. But unlike oil, it never runs out, and it grows more valuable every time it is combined with other data.

hero.hook: Facebook can guess that you are about to get married or move house before you are aware of it yourself.

blocks.text: One phrase has stuck since the 2010s: **data** is “the oil of the 21st century.” The idea is simple. Once refined by algorithms, data becomes the engine of growth and of global power.

But oil is a resource that runs out, and data is not. It can be copied endlessly, and it grows more valuable each time it is matched against other information. Here is why it has redrawn the world economy.

sections.title: Predicting our behavior before we do

blocks.text: The real value of data does not lie in a plain list of names or addresses. It lies in the power to predict what we will do next. Every search, every trip, every click leaves a trace, and technology companies gather those traces into a very precise portrait of each person.
Facebook can spot a major life change, a coming wedding or a move to a new home, before the person involved is fully aware of it, simply by picking up small shifts in their online habits.

This systematic mining of our behavior created what the researcher Shoshana Zuboff calls **surveillance capitalism**. People are no longer only customers. They become the raw material of a system that sells predictions to the highest bidder.

sections.title: Why these giants are almost impossible to challenge

blocks.text: The data economy runs on a virtuous circle: the more data a company holds, the better its service gets, which attracts more users, who generate still more data. Artificial intelligence has sped that up. A [[machine learning]] algorithm trained on billions of examples becomes more accurate, and improves faster, than a rival with limited resources.

blocks.caption: Data centers use as much electricity as entire cities to handle these huge flows of information

blocks.text: These giants, the [[GAFAM]] in the United States and the BATX in China, no longer settle for ruling their original sector. They use their lead in data to expand into health, finance and connected cars, locking up access to innovation in many fields.

sections.title: Europe strikes back with the GDPR

blocks.text: Faced with that power, in 2018 the European Union brought in [[The European GDPR]], a regulation that in theory hands citizens back control over their own personal information: transparency, the right to be forgotten, and mandatory consent.

Its strength comes from reaching beyond Europe's borders: any company that handles the data of European citizens has to comply, or face fines of up to 4% of its worldwide revenue. That pushed giants like Meta and Amazon to change their practices everywhere, and made Europe a global regulator almost by accident.
Before the GDPR forced companies to be clear, an ordinary person would have needed about 76 working days to read every terms-of-service document they agreed to in a single year.

sections.title: Data as a question of sovereignty

blocks.text: Beyond the economy, data has become a tool of power for states themselves, which can use it to watch their own population or steer public opinion. Countries unable to protect their citizens' data risk a form of technological dependence, a direct blow to their [[digital sovereignty]].

The great challenge of the coming decades will be to balance the progress that large-scale data analysis makes possible against privacy, the basic condition of individual freedom in an ever more connected society.

Data has become a strategic asset whose value comes from its power to predict what we will do. This economy favors technology giants that are almost impossible to challenge, and Europe's answer is strict regulation: the GDPR.
